bestseller = a book that sells in very large numbers
sequel = a book or film that continues an earlier story
prequel = a story set before the events of the original
autobiography = a book a person writes about their own life
biography = a book about another person's life, written by someone else
memoir = a personal account of a period in the writer's life
satire = writing that uses humour to criticise people or institutions
metaphor = a figure of speech that describes something as if it were something else
protagonist = the main character in a story
antagonist = the character who opposes the main character
narrator = the voice that tells the story
plot twist = a sudden, surprising change in the story
cliffhanger = an ending that leaves the audience waiting to know what happens
anthology = a collection of poems, stories or extracts by different writers
prose = ordinary written language, not poetry
sonnet = a fourteen-line poem with a set rhyme pattern
fable = a short story, often with animals, that teaches a moral
allegory = a story whose characters and events stand for ideas
irony = a contrast between what is said or expected and what is meant or happens
theme = a central idea that a work of art explores
manuscript = the original typed or handwritten version of a text
publisher = a company that prepares and sells books
ghostwriter = a person who writes a book that is published under someone else's name
book signing = an event where an author signs copies for readers
literary critic = a person who writes professional judgements of books
coming-of-age novel = a novel about a young person growing into adulthood
historical fiction = a novel set in the past, mixing invented characters with real events
dystopian fiction = stories set in an imagined society that has gone badly wrong
page-turner = a book so interesting that you want to keep reading
banned book = a book that authorities have forbidden people to read or sell
commemorate = to honour the memory of a person or event
premiere = the first public showing of a film, play or work
box office = the place that sells tickets; the money a film takes
blockbuster = a very popular film that makes a huge amount of money
box-office flop = a film that fails to make much money
arthouse cinema = films made for artistic value rather than mass entertainment
film festival = an event where new films are shown and often judged
cinematography = the art of camera work and lighting in a film
screenplay = the written script of a film, including dialogue and action
film adaptation = a film based on a book, play or other work
remake = a new version of an earlier film
biopic = a film that tells the life story of a real person
period drama = a film or series set in a historical period, with period clothes
close-up = a shot that shows a face or object in great detail
voice-over = speech heard on the soundtrack while someone else is shown
dubbing = replacing the original speech in a film with another language
subtitles = words on the screen that translate or transcribe the speech
cameo = a brief appearance by a well-known person in a film
typecast = repeatedly given the same kind of acting role
cult film = a film with a small but very devoted group of fans
independent film = a film made outside the major studios, often on a low budget
stunt double = a performer who does dangerous scenes in place of an actor
supporting role = an important acting part that is not the lead
leading role = the main acting part in a film or play
feature film = a full-length film, usually over about ninety minutes
short film = a film lasting only a few minutes to about forty minutes
thriller = a film or book meant to keep you tense and excited
genre = a category of art with shared features, such as comedy or horror
film critic = a person who writes professional reviews of films
age rating = an official label showing the minimum age for a film
slow motion = a film effect that makes movement appear slower than real life
end credits = the list of names shown after a film finishes
audience = the people watching a play, film or concert
rehearsal = a practice session before a public performance
dress rehearsal = the final rehearsal in costume, as if it were the real show
encore = an extra song or piece performed after the planned end
standing ovation = when the whole audience stands up and claps
understudy = an actor who learns a role in case the main actor cannot perform
matinee = an afternoon performance of a play or film
opening night = the first public performance of a play or show
stalls = the seats on the ground floor of a theatre
dress circle = the first raised seating level in a theatre
usher = a person who shows people to their seats in a theatre or cinema
interval = a short break in the middle of a play or concert
curtain call = when the cast return to the stage to receive applause
soliloquy = a speech in which a character speaks thoughts aloud, alone on stage
monologue = a long speech by one person in a play or performance
improvisation = performing without a prepared script
stage fright = nervousness before or during a public performance
playwright = a person who writes plays
scenery = the painted backgrounds and structures on a stage
props = objects that actors use on stage or on set
backstage = the area behind the stage, not seen by the audience
tragedy = a serious play with a sad ending, often about a hero's downfall
farce = a comic play based on ridiculous situations and mistakes
West End = London's main commercial theatre district
fringe theatre = small, experimental theatre outside the commercial mainstream
amateur dramatics = theatre performed by non-professionals, often locally
orchestra pit = the lowered area in front of the stage where musicians play
piracy = illegal copying or sharing of films, music or books
symphony = a long piece of music for a full orchestra, usually in several movements
concerto = a piece for a solo instrument with orchestral accompaniment
chamber music = classical music for a small group of players, often one to a part
aria = a song for one voice in an opera, with orchestral accompaniment
virtuoso = a musician of outstanding technical skill
cover version = a new recording of a song first performed by someone else
busker = a musician who performs in the street for money
acoustic = played without electronic amplification
headliner = the main act that a concert or festival is built around
support act = a band or singer who performs before the main artist
gig = an informal word for a concert, especially of popular music
concert venue = the building or site where a concert is held
sheet music = printed music showing the notes to play or sing
recording studio = a room designed for recording music or sound
record label = a company that produces and markets recorded music
vinyl = music pressed on a plastic disc, often collected again today
arts funding = public or private money given to support the arts
book club = a group that meets to discuss a book they have all read
jam session = an informal session in which musicians improvise together
live album = a recording of music performed in front of an audience
chart-topping = reaching the highest position on the music charts
intangible heritage = traditions, skills and practices passed down, not buildings
freedom of expression = the right to say, write or create without unfair restriction
still life = a picture of arranged objects such as fruit, flowers or crockery
abstract art = art that does not try to show things as they look in real life
impressionism = a nineteenth-century style that captures light and a moment's impression
cubism = an early twentieth-century style showing objects from several angles at once
surrealism = art that mixes dream images with unexpected, illogical combinations
Renaissance = the European revival of classical art and learning, roughly 14th–16th centuries
watercolour = paint that is mixed with water; a picture made with it
fresco = a painting done on wet plaster, usually on a wall or ceiling
mural = a large painting on a wall, often in a public place
collage = art made by sticking different materials onto a surface
installation art = a three-dimensional artwork designed for a particular space
contemporary art = art being made in the present period
street art = art in public spaces, including murals and stencils, often unsanctioned
graffiti = writing or drawings, often sprayed, on walls in public places
pop art = mid-twentieth-century art that uses images from advertising and mass culture
canvas = a strong cloth surface on which oil paintings are usually made
palette = the board on which an artist mixes colours; the range of colours used
composition = the way shapes, colours and figures are arranged in a work of art
perspective = the technique of drawing objects so they appear to recede in space
self-portrait = a picture an artist makes of themselves
art collector = a person who buys artworks, often as an investment or passion
forgery = a fake artwork made to look like the work of a famous artist
restoration = repairing and cleaning an artwork or historic object
broadsheet = a serious newspaper, traditionally printed on large sheets
tabloid = a popular newspaper with short articles, big headlines and many photos
bias = an unfair preference for or against a person, group or idea
breaking news = news that is just coming in and is being reported immediately
streaming = watching or listening to media over the internet as it is sent
paywall = a system that allows only paying users to read or watch content
influencer = a person who promotes products or views to a large online following
headline = the title of a newspaper article, printed in large letters
editorial = an article that gives the newspaper's own opinion
investigative journalism = reporting that uncovers hidden facts, often over a long period
correspondent = a journalist who reports from a particular place or on a particular topic
press conference = a meeting where someone answers journalists' questions
exclusive = a story published or broadcast by only one news organisation
fake news = false stories presented as news, often to mislead or attract clicks
misinformation = false or inaccurate information, whether spread on purpose or not
clickbait = a sensational headline designed to make people click, often misleading
sensationalism = presenting stories in an exaggerated way to shock or excite
freedom of the press = the right of newspapers and broadcasters to report without unfair control
prime time = the evening hours when the largest television audience is watching
readership = the people who regularly read a newspaper or magazine
paparazzi = photographers who aggressively pursue celebrities for pictures
podcast = a spoken audio programme you can download or stream in episodes
going viral = spreading extremely quickly across the internet
echo chamber = an online space where you only meet opinions you already agree with
binge-watching = watching many episodes of a series one after another
subscription = a regular payment that gives access to a service or publication
mass media = newspapers, television, radio and large websites that reach huge audiences
public service broadcasting = radio and television funded to inform, educate and entertain, not only to profit
listed building = a historic building legally protected from harmful alteration
folklore = the traditional stories, songs, customs and beliefs of a community
high culture = art forms traditionally seen as serious and elite, such as opera and classical music
popular culture = entertainment and fashions enjoyed by large numbers of ordinary people
cultural heritage = the buildings, objects, traditions and knowledge inherited from the past
artefact = an object made by people in the past, of historical interest
UNESCO World Heritage Site = a place recognised internationally as having outstanding cultural or natural value
cultural identity = the sense of belonging to a group that shares language, traditions or history
cultural appropriation = adopting elements of a minority culture in a way many see as disrespectful or exploitative
censorship = official control that forbids or cuts parts of books, films or news
copyright = the legal right to control how a work is copied, performed or sold
intellectual property = legal rights over creations of the mind, such as books, films, designs and inventions
fair dealing = limited legal use of copyrighted material, for example for criticism or teaching
patron of the arts = a person or organisation that gives money to support artists or cultural institutions
commercialisation of culture = turning art and traditions mainly into products to sell
spin = presenting information so that it looks better than it is
